opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth being realistic about where we are. A grand bargain, some comprehensive treaty where both sides agree to cap compute or pause frontier development, isn't on the table right now. The trust isn't there, the verification tools aren't mature enough, and both governments see AI as central to economic and military competitiveness. So if we hold out for that, we'll get nothing.

What I think *is* realistic is a lot more modest, but still valuable. First, there's a shared interest in avoiding catastrophic misuse by third parties. Neither Washington nor Beijing wants non-state actors using AI to develop bioweapons or launch large-scale cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. That's a natural area for at least informal alignment: sharing threat models, agreeing on norms around dangerous capability evaluations, maybe even some technical exchange on how you test for those risks.

Second, there's value in scientist-to-scientist and lab-to-lab dialogue, the Track 2 stuff. Historically, during the Cold War, a lot of the groundwork for arms control came from scientists talking to each other before the governments were ready. I think we can build a shared vocabulary about what loss of control looks like, what alignment failures look like, what red lines might make sense, so that if there's a moment when political will appears, the intellectual infrastructure already exists.

Third, and this is where my own research interests come in, we should invest heavily in verification technology now. Things like hardware-enabled mechanisms on chips, compute accounting, ways to attest what training runs happened without revealing sensitive IP. A lot of the pessimism about coordination comes from "we can't trust them and we can't check." If you make checking cheaper, the space of feasible agreements grows a lot.

And I'd push back a little on the race-to-the-bottom framing being inevitable. Safety isn't purely a cost. A system that's unreliable, that can be jailbroken, that behaves unpredictably, is less useful to a military or an economy, not more. Neither side benefits from deploying something they can't control. So part of the work is making that case clearly, so that safety is seen as a component of capability rather than a tax on it.

So the realistic version is: narrow agreements on shared catastrophic risks, sustained technical dialogue, and building the verification tools that would make deeper cooperation possible later. It's not glamorous, but it keeps options open, and that matters a lot given how fast things are moving.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I'm actually more optimistic about this than a lot of people in the field, but optimistic in a fairly narrow sense. I don't think we're going to get some grand treaty where the US and China agree to jointly pause frontier development or hand oversight to an international body. That's just not where the geopolitics are. But I also don't think we need that for the most important failure modes.

If you look at where the two countries' interests actually overlap, there's quite a lot. Neither government wants a model that can autonomously conduct cyberattacks to leak out and end up in the hands of non-state actors. Neither wants an AI-enabled bioweapons capability floating around. And neither wants to lose control of a system that's doing something they didn't intend. Those are areas where the incentives aren't zero-sum. A loss of control event in Beijing is bad for Washington too, and vice versa. So that's where I'd focus.

Concretely, I think the realistic near-term stuff looks like, one, agreement on a small number of red lines around specific dangerous capabilities, things like uplift for weapons of mass destruction or self-replication, where both sides commit to evaluating for them and not deploying systems that cross them. Two, some shared technical standards for how you do those evaluations, because right now everyone's doing something different and that makes any kind of mutual verification impossible. And three, honestly just communication channels. Having scientists and officials who know each other and talk regularly, so that if something goes wrong, there's a phone to pick up. That sounds trivial but we had a version of it during the Cold War and it mattered.

The harder question is verification. A commitment to not train past some threshold is only meaningful if the other side can check, and the compute governance ideas there are still fairly immature. I'd put more weight on things that are self-enforcing or where you can verify through the deployment rather than the training. If you're releasing a model publicly, people can red-team it. That's a form of verification that doesn't require trusting the other party's internal processes.

The thing I'd push back on a bit is the framing that it's purely a race to the bottom. Both countries have domestic reasons to want safety. China's actually been fairly aggressive about regulating consumer-facing AI, for its own reasons, but those reasons still produce safety-relevant behavior. So I think the goal of coordination is less about creating safety incentives from scratch and more about making sure that competitive pressure doesn't erode the ones that already exist. And that's a more tractable problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the most realistic starting point is agreement on fairly concrete safety practices, rather than trying to agree on an entire approach to AI governance. The US and China have substantial disagreements, and those aren't going away. But neither side benefits from developing systems that they can't reliably control.

So, for example, can we establish a shared understanding of how to evaluate dangerous capabilities? Can we agree that certain findings should trigger additional testing or security precautions before deployment? You could have technical collaboration on evaluation methods without requiring either side to share model weights or strategically sensitive information.

The difficult part is verification. An agreement that says, “We'll both take safety seriously,” doesn't do much if each side believes the other is cutting corners. You want commitments that are specific enough that there's some way to assess whether they're being followed, and where following them doesn't put you at a huge competitive disadvantage.

I'd also distinguish coordination from waiting for consensus. The US can implement sensible safety requirements domestically while pursuing reciprocal commitments from China. Ideally, that creates a floor underneath the competition: you can compete on how capable and useful your systems are, but there are some safety shortcuts that neither side takes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most realistic starting point is fairly narrow coordination around risks that both countries would prefer to avoid. Neither the US nor China wants to lose control of a powerful AI system, and neither benefits from an accident that has consequences across borders. That gives you some common ground, even if there’s deep disagreement about how AI should be used.

I’d start with things like shared evaluation methods, exchanging information about serious safety incidents, and establishing channels so that an unexpected event doesn’t immediately get interpreted as a hostile action. You don’t need to share model weights or sensitive capabilities research to compare how you test whether a system can evade oversight, for example.

The harder step is agreeing that certain findings should trigger a pause or additional safeguards. That requires some ability to verify what the other side is doing. So I’m skeptical of an agreement that just says, ‘We’ll both develop AI responsibly.’ You want specific commitments where compliance is observable, and where each side has a reason to comply even if trust is limited.

And I wouldn’t make domestic safety policy contingent on getting an agreement with China. We should build the capacity to evaluate and secure these systems anyway. International coordination can then help keep competitive pressure from eroding those protections.
